state.misconception_label: Confuses rest and movement on a distance time graph

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: This graph shows how far Fido the dog is from his home. What might the negative-sloping section represent? ![A graph with time (secs) on the horizontal axis and distance (m) on the vertical axis. The graph starts at the origin, travels in a straight line up and right, travels horizontally, then travels in a straight line down and right back to the x-axis. ](). I got Fido has fallen asleep because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine Fido is on a walk and the negative-sloping section represents him walking away from home. Just like how the graph shows his distance decreasing from his starting point. Let's think about how the movement on the graph relates to Fido's actual actions in the real world.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh wait, so when the line goes down, that means the distance is getting smaller, so Fido must be walking *back towards* his home, not away from it? But I'm still a bit confused - why would the line going down mean he's moving closer instead of like, moving backwards or something?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think about when you're walking back home from a friend's house. Even though you're moving in the opposite direction from when you walked away, you're still getting closer to your house. The same idea applies to Fido on the graph - when the line goes down, he's getting closer to his starting point, just like when you walk back home.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher initially gives incorrect information (Turn 1 says negative slope means walking away from home, which is wrong), then corrects it through analogy rather than addressing the rest/movement confusion directly; the student shows some progress but still expresses confusion about the meaning of the downward slope.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently grounds the abstract graph interpretation in concrete, relatable scenarios (Fido walking, walking back from a friend's house) and explicitly connects the mathematical representation to everyday physical movement experiences.
